chunks.heading: What is a force?
chunks.body: A force is a push or a pull. It can start an object moving, stop it, speed it up, slow it down, or change its direction.
chunks.checkText: A force is best described as a...

chunks.heading: Touching forces and forces at a distance
chunks.body: A contact force needs the objects to be touching, like a kick on a ball. A field force, like gravity or magnetism, can act without touching.
chunks.checkText: Gravity is an example of a...

chunks.heading: Adding up all the forces
chunks.body: When several [[phys-force-def|forces]] act on an object at once, the net force is the sum of all of them combined into one single force.
chunks.checkText: The net force on an object is...

checkOptions.text: The combined sum of all forces acting on it

chunks.heading: When forces cancel out
chunks.body: Equilibrium happens when the [[phys-net-force|net force]] on an object is zero, because all the forces on it balance each other out.
chunks.checkText: An object is in equilibrium when its net force is...

chunks.heading: Newton's first law
chunks.body: Newton's first law says an object keeps a constant velocity unless an unbalanced force acts on it. A resting object stays at rest, a moving one keeps moving.
chunks.checkText: According to Newton's first law, an object's velocity changes only when...

checkOptions.text: An unbalanced force acts on it
It stays still for too long

chunks.heading: Inertia: resisting a change in motion
chunks.body: Inertia is an object's tendency to resist a change in its motion. A heavier object has more inertia, so it's harder to speed up, slow down, or turn.
chunks.checkText: An object with a large mass has...

checkOptions.text: Less inertia than a light object

chunks.heading: Terminal velocity
chunks.body: As a falling object speeds up, air resistance pushes back harder. Terminal velocity is reached when air resistance balances gravity, so the object stops accelerating.
chunks.checkText: Terminal velocity is reached when...

checkOptions.text: Air resistance balances the pull of gravity

chunks.heading: Newton's second law
chunks.body: Newton's second law says force equals mass times acceleration: F = ma. A bigger force or a smaller mass both produce a bigger acceleration.
chunks.checkText: Newton's second law is written as...

chunks.heading: The newton: a unit of force
chunks.body: Force is measured in newtons (N). One newton is the force needed to accelerate a 1 kg mass at 1 m/s^2.
chunks.checkText: The SI unit for force is the...

chunks.heading: Bigger force, bigger acceleration
chunks.body: For a fixed mass, applying a bigger [[phys-force-def|force]] causes a bigger acceleration. Doubling the force doubles the acceleration.
chunks.checkText: If you double the force on a fixed mass, its acceleration...

chunks.heading: Bigger mass, smaller acceleration
chunks.body: For a fixed force, a bigger mass produces a smaller acceleration. Doubling the mass halves the acceleration.
chunks.checkText: If you double an object's mass while the force stays the same, its acceleration...

chunks.heading: Mass and weight aren't the same thing
chunks.body: Mass is how much matter an object has, measured in kilograms. Weight is the force of gravity on that mass, measured in newtons: weight = mg.
chunks.checkText: Weight is measured in which unit?

chunks.heading: Why a feather and a hammer fall together
chunks.body: Without air resistance, all objects accelerate at the same rate when they fall, no matter their mass. A bigger mass also needs a bigger [[phys-mass-vs-weight|weight]] force to move it, so the two effects cancel out.
chunks.checkText: Ignoring air resistance, a heavy object and a light object dropped together will...

checkOptions.text: Hit the ground at the same time

chunks.heading: Why a feather really falls slower
chunks.body: On Earth, air resistance affects light objects much more than heavy ones. That's why a feather drifts down slowly while a hammer falls fast.
chunks.checkText: Air resistance has the biggest effect on falling objects that are...

checkOptions.text: Light, with a large surface area

chunks.heading: Newton's third law
chunks.body: Newton's third law says every action force has an equal and opposite reaction force. If you push on something, it pushes back on you just as hard.
chunks.checkText: Newton's third law says every action force has...

checkOptions.text: An equal and opposite reaction force

chunks.heading: Action and reaction act on different objects
chunks.body: In an action-reaction pair, the two forces always act on two different objects, never on the same one. That's why they can't cancel each other out.
chunks.checkText: The action and reaction forces in a pair act on...

chunks.heading: The normal force
chunks.body: When an object rests on a surface, the surface pushes back on it. This push, at right angles to the surface, is called the normal force.
chunks.checkText: The normal force always acts...

checkOptions.text: At right angles to the surface
In the same direction as gravity

chunks.heading: A common mix-up: weight and normal force
chunks.body: Weight and the [[phys-normal-force|normal force]] on a resting object are equal and opposite, but they are not a Newton's third law pair, because both act on the same object.
chunks.checkText: Weight and normal force on a resting book are not a Newton's third law pair because...

checkOptions.text: They both act on the same object
They point in the same direction
One of them isn't a real force

chunks.heading: Forces on a slope
chunks.body: On a tilted surface, the [[phys-normal-force|normal force]] shrinks as the angle increases, while more of the weight pulls the object down along the slope.
chunks.checkText: As a slope gets steeper, the normal force acting on an object on it...

chunks.heading: Friction: a force that resists sliding
chunks.body: Friction is a force between two touching surfaces that opposes their movement relative to each other. It always acts against the direction of motion.
chunks.checkText: Friction always acts...

checkOptions.text: In the same direction as motion

chunks.heading: Two kinds of friction
chunks.body: Static [[phys-friction-def|friction]] stops an object from starting to slide. Once it's moving, kinetic friction takes over, and it's usually weaker than static friction.
chunks.checkText: Which type of friction is usually stronger?

chunks.heading: The coefficient of friction
chunks.body: The coefficient of friction is a number that shows how much [[phys-friction-def|friction]] exists between two particular surfaces. Rougher surfaces give a higher number.
chunks.checkText: A higher coefficient of friction means the surfaces are...

checkOptions.text: Rougher, with more friction between them

chunks.heading: Calculating friction
chunks.body: The friction force equals the [[phys-coefficient-of-friction|coefficient of friction]] multiplied by the [[phys-normal-force|normal force]] pressing the surfaces together.
chunks.checkText: To calculate the friction force, you multiply the coefficient of friction by the...

chunks.heading: What is energy?
chunks.body: Energy is the capacity to cause change. Anything that can push, lift, heat, or move something else has energy.
chunks.checkText: Energy is best described as the capacity to...

chunks.heading: Kinetic energy: the energy of motion
chunks.body: Kinetic energy is [[phys-energy-def|energy]] that a moving object has. The faster something moves, or the more mass it has, the more kinetic energy it carries.
chunks.checkText: Kinetic energy is energy associated with...

chunks.heading: Potential energy: stored energy
chunks.body: Potential energy is [[phys-energy-def|energy]] stored because of an object's position, like a ball held up high, ready to fall.
chunks.checkText: Potential energy depends on an object's...

chunks.heading: The joule: a unit of energy
chunks.body: Energy and work are both measured in joules (J). One joule is roughly the energy needed to lift a small apple by 10 centimetres.
chunks.checkText: Energy is measured using which unit?

chunks.heading: What is work?
chunks.body: Work is done when a force moves an object. It equals the net force multiplied by the distance moved in the force's direction: W = Fs.
chunks.checkText: Work is defined as force multiplied by...

checkOptions.text: Distance moved in the force's direction

chunks.heading: No movement means no work
chunks.body: If a force is applied but the object doesn't move, no [[phys-work-def|work]] is done, even if it takes a lot of effort, like holding a heavy bag still.
chunks.checkText: If you push against a wall and it doesn't move, how much work do you do on the wall?

checkOptions.text: It depends only on how hard you push

chunks.heading: Work when the force is at an angle
chunks.body: If a force acts at an angle to the direction of movement, only the part of the force pointing along the motion actually does [[phys-work-def|work]].
chunks.checkText: When a force is applied at an angle to an object's motion, the work done depends on...

checkOptions.text: Only the part of the force along the direction of motion
The entire force, regardless of angle
Only the part of the force at right angles to motion

chunks.heading: Calculating kinetic energy
chunks.body: The [[phys-kinetic-energy-intro|kinetic energy]] of an object is given by K = 1/2 mv^2, where m is mass and v is speed.
chunks.checkText: The formula for kinetic energy is...

chunks.heading: Work changes kinetic energy
chunks.body: The work-energy theorem says the [[phys-work-def|work]] done on an object equals its change in [[phys-kinetic-energy-formula|kinetic energy]].
chunks.checkText: The work-energy theorem links work done to a change in...

chunks.heading: Calculating gravitational potential energy
chunks.body: The change in gravitational [[phys-potential-energy-intro|potential energy]] of an object equals its mass times g times the height it rises: change in PE = mgh.
chunks.checkText: The formula for the change in gravitational potential energy is...

chunks.heading: Choosing a starting point for height
chunks.body: Gravitational [[phys-potential-energy-intro|potential energy]] is always measured relative to a chosen reference level, like the ground or a tabletop. Only the height change from that level matters.
chunks.checkText: Gravitational potential energy is always calculated relative to...

checkOptions.text: The centre of the Earth only
Nothing — it has no reference point

chunks.heading: Mechanical energy: kinetic plus potential
chunks.body: Mechanical energy is the sum of an object's [[phys-kinetic-energy-intro|kinetic energy]] and [[phys-potential-energy-intro|potential energy]].
chunks.checkText: Mechanical energy is the sum of an object's kinetic energy and its...

chunks.heading: Mechanical energy stays constant
chunks.body: When only gravity acts on a falling object, its [[phys-mechanical-energy-def|mechanical energy]] stays the same. As potential energy drops, kinetic energy rises by the same amount.
chunks.checkText: As a falling object loses gravitational potential energy, its kinetic energy...

chunks.heading: How fast is a falling object going?
chunks.body: Using [[phys-conservation-of-mechanical-energy|conservation of mechanical energy]], the speed of a falling object is v = sqrt(2gh), no matter its mass.
chunks.checkText: The formula for the speed of an object that has fallen a height h is...

chunks.heading: When mechanical energy isn't conserved
chunks.body: Real bouncing balls lose a little [[phys-mechanical-energy-def|mechanical energy]] on each bounce, as some of it turns into heat and sound. That's why each bounce is lower than the last.
chunks.checkText: A bouncing ball gets lower with each bounce because some mechanical energy is turned into...

chunks.heading: Power: how fast work is done
chunks.body: Power measures how quickly [[phys-work-def|work]] is done or energy is transferred. It's calculated as power = energy transferred divided by time taken.
chunks.checkText: Power is a measure of...

chunks.heading: The watt: a unit of power
chunks.body: [[phys-power-def|Power]] is measured in watts (W). One watt equals one joule of energy transferred every second.
chunks.checkText: One watt is equal to...

chunks.heading: Power from force and speed
chunks.body: When something moves at a constant speed against a force, [[phys-power-def|power]] can also be found using P = Fv, force multiplied by velocity.
chunks.checkText: For an object moving at constant speed, power can be calculated as force multiplied by...

chunks.heading: Resistance that slows things down
chunks.body: Rolling resistance comes from a wheel's contact with the ground, while air resistance comes from air pushing back on a moving object. Both oppose motion and reduce speed.
chunks.checkText: Rolling resistance is caused by...

checkOptions.text: A wheel's contact with the ground
Air pushing on a moving object

chunks.heading: What is momentum?
chunks.body: Momentum is a measure of how hard it is to stop a moving object. It equals mass times velocity: p = mv.
chunks.checkText: The formula for momentum is...

chunks.heading: Momentum has a direction
chunks.body: Because velocity is a vector, [[phys-momentum-def|momentum]] is a vector too. It has both a size and a direction, not just a number.
chunks.checkText: Momentum is a vector, which means it has...

checkOptions.text: Both a size and a direction

chunks.heading: Momentum is conserved
chunks.body: In any collision, the total [[phys-momentum-def|momentum]] of a closed system before the collision equals the total momentum after it.
chunks.checkText: The law of conservation of momentum says total momentum before a collision...

chunks.heading: When objects bounce apart
chunks.body: If two objects collide and bounce apart, [[phys-conservation-of-momentum|conservation of momentum]] gives m1u1 + m2u2 = m1v1 + m2v2, with u for initial and v for final velocities.
chunks.checkText: In a collision where two objects bounce apart and stay separate, the correct equation is...

chunks.heading: When objects stick together
chunks.body: If two objects collide and stick together, [[phys-conservation-of-momentum|conservation of momentum]] gives m1u1 + m2u2 = (m1 + m2)v, using one final velocity for the combined mass.
chunks.checkText: When two colliding objects stick together afterwards, they share...

chunks.heading: When one object splits into two
chunks.body: In an explosive collision, one object breaks into two pieces. [[phys-conservation-of-momentum|Conservation of momentum]] still applies: the total momentum before equals the total after.
chunks.checkText: An explosive collision is one where...

checkOptions.text: One object breaks apart into two pieces

chunks.heading: Elastic collisions keep their energy
chunks.body: In an elastic collision, total kinetic energy before the collision equals total kinetic energy after it. No energy is lost to heat or sound.
chunks.checkText: In an elastic collision, kinetic energy is...

chunks.heading: Inelastic collisions lose energy
chunks.body: In an inelastic collision, unlike an [[phys-elastic-collision|elastic collision]], some kinetic energy is converted into other forms like heat and sound, so total kinetic energy after is less than before.
chunks.checkText: In an inelastic collision, some kinetic energy is...

chunks.heading: Impulse: a change in momentum
chunks.body: Impulse is the change in an object's [[phys-momentum-def|momentum]]. It's calculated as final momentum minus initial momentum: impulse = mv - mu.
chunks.checkText: Impulse is defined as the...

chunks.heading: Change in momentum when direction changes
chunks.body: When an object changes direction, not just speed, its [[phys-impulse-def|change in momentum]] can be found by drawing the initial and final velocity vectors and using geometry.
chunks.checkText: To find a change in momentum when direction also changes, you can use...

chunks.heading: Impulse from force and time
chunks.body: From Newton's second law, [[phys-impulse-def|impulse]] also equals net force multiplied by the time it acts: impulse = F x t.
chunks.checkText: Impulse can be calculated as net force multiplied by...

checkOptions.text: The time the force acts for

chunks.heading: Why airbags make crashes safer
chunks.body: For the same [[phys-impulse-force-time|impulse]], spreading the change in momentum over a longer time means a smaller force is needed. This is why airbags and soft landings reduce injury.
chunks.checkText: For the same change in momentum, a longer stopping time results in...

chunks.heading: Reading impulse from a graph
chunks.body: When force changes during a collision, the total [[phys-impulse-def|impulse]] equals the area under a force-versus-time graph.
chunks.checkText: On a force-versus-time graph, the total impulse is equal to...

checkOptions.text: The highest point on the graph
The length of the time axis only
